terms.definition: The pratyagātmā — the inmost Self that cannot be objectified — is the subject matter (viṣaya) of brahmavidyā.
terms.context: Swamiji explains that brahmavidyā is not knowledge of some external Brahman but of oneself as Brahman. Because brahmavidyā removes the false notion 'I am a body or mind,' its subject matter must be the very Self which underlies all such notions. Śaṅkara quotes Bṛh. Up. 1.4.10 — 'tadātmānamevāved ahaṃ brahmāsmīti' — to show that once one knows the Self thus, one becomes everything, since there is no second reality.

terms.definition: 'These three — name, form, and function — constitute everything that is.' (Bṛh. Up. 1.6.1)
terms.context: Swamiji uses this as the Upaniṣad's own summary of the manifest world. Whatever can be objectified has a name (nāma), a form (rūpa), and a function or action (karma). Brahman alone is beyond all three — it is sarvakāraṇam with no nāma-rūpa of its own. The Bhāṣya cites this verse to signal that the entire domain of avidyā has been covered by the first chapter.

terms.definition: Completely free of all distinguishing characteristics; devoid of every qualification.
terms.context: In the Bhāṣya summary of the second chapter, Śaṅkara says that Brahman — taught through neti-neti — is ekam, advayam, and sarvaviśeṣaśūnyam. Swamiji explains viśeṣa as any mark or attribute that distinguishes one thing from another. Since Brahman has no attributes that set it apart from anything, it cannot be grasped as an object. terms.definition: 'Action is not the cause of liberation, just as fire is not the remedy for heat.' (Sureśvarācārya, BV verse 55)

terms.definition: By itself the anātmā (not-self) is non-dear; it comes to be dear only as a means serving one's love for the self.

sectionTitle: Is draṣṭavya a vidhi? — an injunction needs seer/seen difference and a free agent; self-knowledge arises from the sentence itself, so draṣṭavya is only ajñāta-jñāpana, not a call to act

terms.definition: The sole obstacle to apprehending the meaning of a sentence is ignorance of its word-meanings; hence an injunction operates only there — on removing that ignorance — not on producing the knowledge itself.
terms.context: Swamiji: once the words are known, a sentence yields its meaning by itself (vākyādeva); the only thing that blocks vākyārtha-jñāna is not knowing the padārthas. terms.definition: "A person is able to do that, therefore this is enjoined" — śravaṇa, manana and the inner disciplines (śama, dama) lie within human capacity, so it is these ancillary means that injunction prescribes, not self-knowledge itself.
terms.context: Swamiji: since ātma-jñāna is apuruṣatantra (not subject to one's will), a vidhi cannot command it. But śravaṇa (listening), manana (reflection) and śama-dama are puruṣatantra — a person can choose to do them — so the śruti's injunctive force lands on them. One is enjoined to the means; the knowledge then arises of itself.

terms.definition: The love directed at son, wealth, and objects that comes 'by way of deviation' — transient, conditional affection that arises and passes with its object, as opposed to the constant, intrinsic love for the self.
terms.context: Swamiji glosses yā prītiḥ abhicāreṇa putrādau: abhicāra means 'subject to going', deviating. The love we place on the apple-form, music-form, taste-form appears and disappears with the object, whereas prīti for the ātmā is avyabhicārī — never deviating. Seeing this transience is the basis of vairāgya and karma-yoga.

sectionTitle: Kinds of Vidhi (apūrva / niyama / parisaṃkhyā) and why none applies to brahma-vidyā — Vidyāraṇya's Vārtikasāra 40–59: consciousness is nitya-prāpta, every vṛtti is cidākṛti, and pramāṇa-born knowledge is indispensable

terms.definition: Apūrva-vidhi — an injunction that enjoins something entirely unattained by any other means (atyanta-aprāpti); it conveys a wholly new, otherwise-unavailable thing.
terms.context: From the Mīmāṃsā threefold classification of vidhi that Swamiji introduced (apūrva, niyama, parisaṃkhyā) to show none applies to brahma-vidyā. Apūrva-vidhi operates 'atyantam aprāptau' — where the result is not available otherwise (e.g. agnihotraṃ juhuyāt). Brahman, being nitya-prāpta (ever-attained), is never apūrva.

terms.definition: Niyama-vidhi — a restrictive injunction that operates when there is an option (pākṣika): the end is attainable in more than one way and the vidhi fixes one of them.
terms.context: The second of the three.
